title: Organolithium and Grignard reagents
goals: Explain why the carbon of a C-Li or C-Mg bond carries a partial negative charge
Write the preparation of an organolithium reagent and of a Grignard reagent, with the metal, the number of equivalents and the solvent
Draw the mechanism of methyllithium with water and use pKa values to show that it goes to completion
Plan a short synthesis that places H or D on a chosen carbon
Draw the mechanism of a Grignard reagent with carbon dioxide followed by acid, as on the past exam

sections.title: A carbon-metal bond is polarized toward carbon
sections.html:
The acids lecture ended with a problem: the methyl anion is a very strong base, and no ordinary base can make it from methane. Organometallic reagents, compounds with a carbon-metal bond, are the solution. The lecture introduces two kinds, and the first is the organolithium reagent, R-Li, where R is a hydrocarbon group.

Everything about these reagents follows from the direction in which the bond is polarized:

[[mol:[Li]C|me]] [[mol:CCl|me]]
BondCarbonPartnerHow to think of it
{{H3C-Li}}δ−Li, δ+{{H3C-}} with {{Li+}}
{{H3C-Cl}}δ+Cl, δ−polarized the other way
{{H3C-Br}}δ+Br, δ−polar, but not ionic

In an alkyl halide the carbon is the positive end of the bond. In methyllithium the carbon is the negative end. The instruction in the notes is to think of {{H3C-Li}} as {{H3C-}} and {{Li+}}: a carbon with a lone pair and a negative charge, next to a metal cation.

The notes add an aside for comparison, lithium hydroxide: HO-Li ⇌ {{HO-}} + {{Li+}}. A bond from lithium to oxygen is fully ionic, and nobody hesitates to write hydroxide as a free anion. The bond from lithium to carbon is treated in the same spirit: the carbon behaves as a carbanion.

micro.h: The electrons of a bond sit closer to the more electronegative atom. Approximate electronegativities: Li 1.0, Mg 1.3, C 2.5, Br 3.0, Cl 3.2. Carbon is more electronegative than either metal, so in C-Li and C-Mg the shared pair lies toward carbon, and carbon is δ−. Carbon is less electronegative than the halogens, so in C-Cl and C-Br the pair lies toward the halogen, and carbon is δ+. The difference between C and Li, about 1.5, is much larger than the difference between C and Br, about 0.5. That is why the lecture calls {{H3C-Br}} not ionic but asks you to think of {{H3C-Li}} as ions.

macro.t: The same carbon, with its reactivity reversed
macro.h: In the next lecture pages the carbon of {{H3C-Cl}} is the electrophile: hydroxide attacks it and chloride leaves, which is the {{SN2}} reaction. Replace the halogen with a metal and the same carbon becomes the electron-rich partner, a base and a nucleophile. This reversal is one of the most useful ideas in organic synthesis, because joining an electron-rich carbon to an electron-poor carbon makes a new carbon-carbon bond. The past exam uses it in Question 1D, where the carbon of a Grignard reagent attacks carbon dioxide.

why.q: Why is the carbon of methyllithium partially negative when the carbon of chloromethane is partially positive?
why.a: Bonding electrons are pulled toward the more electronegative atom. Carbon is more electronegative than lithium, so it takes the larger share of the C-Li pair. Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, so in C-Cl the pair is pulled away from carbon.

sections.title: Making an organolithium reagent: R-Br, two equivalents of lithium, pentane
sections.html:
Organolithium reagents are made from alkyl halides and lithium metal. The recipe in the notes:

R-Br (or R-Cl) + {{Li}}0 (2 equivalents), in pentane → R-Li + LiBr

For example, with 1-bromobutane:

[[rxn:CCCCBr>2 Li;pentane>CCCC[Li] + [Li+].[Br-]]]

Read each part of the recipe:

  • R-Br or R-Cl. The starting material is an alkyl halide. The carbon that carries the halogen is the carbon that will carry lithium.
  • {{Li}}0. The superscript zero means lithium metal, the neutral element, not a lithium salt.
  • 2 equivalents. Two lithium atoms are used for each molecule of halide. One ends up bonded to carbon in R-Li. The other ends up as {{Li+}} in the salt LiBr.
  • Pentane. The solvent is a plain alkane, which has nothing in it that the product can react with.

Compare the carbon before and after. In R-Br it is δ+, bonded to an electronegative halogen. In R-Li it is δ−, bonded to a metal. The reaction has reversed the polarity of that carbon, and the metal supplied the electrons to do it. This is a different kind of reaction from the proton transfers of the last chapter: electrons move from a metal to the organic molecule.

micro.h: Count electrons. A lithium atom has one valence electron and gives it up easily to become {{Li+}}. To turn R-Br into a carbanion-like R and a bromide ion, the C-Br bonding pair must end up on bromine as {{Br-}}, and carbon needs a new pair of its own. Two electrons are required, so two lithium atoms are required, each giving one. That leaves two {{Li+}} ions: one pairs with the carbon in R-Li and the other pairs with {{Br-}} as LiBr. If a problem shows only one equivalent of lithium, half of the halide is left over.

micro.t: Why the solvent has to be an alkane
micro.h: R-Li behaves as {{R-}}, the conjugate base of an alkane with {{pKa}} 50 to 60. It will take a proton from anything more acidic than that, which includes water (15.7), alcohols (about 16) and even amines (38). A solvent with any O-H or N-H bond would destroy the reagent as fast as it formed. Pentane has only C-H bonds, with the same {{pKa}} as the reagent's own conjugate acid, so there is no driving force for a proton transfer. For the same reason the flask and the halide must be dry.

macro.t: A reagent you prepare, then use
macro.h: Organolithium reagents are not isolated and stored like ordinary compounds. They are prepared in solution, kept away from air and moisture, and used directly in the next step. On an exam this shows up as numbered steps over an arrow: step 1 makes the reagent, step 2 adds whatever it is to react with. Read such a sequence one step at a time and draw the organometallic intermediate, even when the question does not ask for it. In the 11/03 homework, the middle step of the synthesis is exactly this preparation.

why.q: Why does the preparation need two equivalents of lithium and not one?
why.a: Each lithium atom can give only one electron, and converting R-Br into R-Li and bromide takes two electrons: the carbon changes from the positive end of a bond to the negative end. One lithium becomes the Li of R-Li and the other becomes the Li+ of LiBr.

sections.title: Making a Grignard reagent: R-X and magnesium in diethyl ether
sections.html:
The second kind of organometallic reagent is the Grignard reagent, R-Mg-X, where X is a halogen. The way to think about it is written beside the formula: R:− (MgX)+ → a strong base. Once again the carbon carries the electron pair.

The recipe:

R-X + {{Mg}}0 in diethyl ether → R-MgX

For example, with 2-bromopropane:

[[rxn:CC(C)Br>Mg;diethyl ether>CC(C)[Mg]Br]]

The magnesium atom ends up between the carbon and the halogen. Nothing is lost: every atom of the halide and the magnesium atom are in the product.

The two preparations side by side:

OrganolithiumGrignard
FormulaR-LiR-Mg-X
Made fromR-Br or R-ClR-X (X = halogen)
Metal{{Li}}0, 2 equivalents{{Mg}}0
Solventpentanediethyl ether
Other productLiBr (or LiCl)none
Think of it as{{R-}} with {{Li+}}R:− with (MgX)+

For the reactions in this course the two reagents do the same job. The 11/03 lecture says so directly: RLi and RMgX both act as R:−.

micro.h: Magnesium is in the second column of the periodic table and has two valence electrons, where lithium has one. The same two electrons are needed here as in the lithium recipe, and a single magnesium atom can supply both, becoming {{Mg^2+}}. Because one metal ion now carries two positive charges, it holds both of the negative partners, the carbon group and the halide, which is why the formula is written R-Mg-X with magnesium in the middle and why no separate salt is formed.

Diethyl ether is chosen for two reasons that come straight from the acids lecture. First, like pentane, it has no acidic hydrogen: only C-H bonds, so the reagent does not destroy it. Second, ether is a Lewis base. The lone pairs on its oxygen are donated to the magnesium, which is electron poor, and this keeps the reagent stable and dissolved. An alcohol would also have lone pairs on oxygen, but its O-H hydrogen ({{pKa}} about 16) would be removed at once by the carbanion. An ether has the lone pairs without the acidic hydrogen.

macro.h: The reagent is named after Victor Grignard, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1912 for it, and it remains one of the standard ways to make carbon-carbon bonds, including in the manufacture of medicines. On the past exam it appears in the highest-valued single part, Question 1D (55 points): phenylmagnesium bromide, PhMgBr, reacts with carbon dioxide and then acid. The first thing to write for that question is the idea from this section: PhMgBr behaves as Ph:− with (MgBr)+.

why.q: Why is a Grignard reagent made in diethyl ether and not in ethanol, which also has an oxygen with lone pairs?
why.a: Ethanol has an O-H hydrogen with a pKa of about 16. The carbon of a Grignard reagent acts as a carbanion, the conjugate base of an acid with pKa 50 to 60, so it would take that proton immediately and become R-H. Ether offers the same stabilizing lone pairs with no acidic hydrogen.

sections.title: Both reagents act as R:⁻, a very strong base: methyllithium and water
sections.html:
The 11/03 lecture finishes the topic with the reaction that defines these reagents. Methyllithium is the base and water is the acid:

[[eqr:[Li]C + O>>C + [Li+].[OH-]]]

{{H3C-Li}} + {{H2O}} ⇌ {{CH4}} + {{Li+}} {{-OH}}

The mechanism has two arrows, and it is an ordinary proton transfer:

[[mech:methyllithium-water]]
  1. The carbon lone pair, which is the electron pair of the C-Li bond, takes H from water, making a new C-H bond.
  2. The H-O electrons go to oxygen, which leaves as hydroxide.

Which way does the equilibrium lie? Use the two {{pKa}} values from the notes:

SideAcid{{pKa}}
leftwaterabout 15.8
rightmethaneabout 50 to 60

The equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid, methane, and the gap is enormous. The lecture's conclusion: these are very strong bases. In practice the reaction goes completely to methane, and the same is true for every R-Li and R-MgX with any O-H acid.

This is why the solvents in the two recipes are pentane and ether, and why water must be kept out until you want the reagent to react with it.

micro.h: K = 10 raised to the power ({{pKa}} of the acid formed − {{pKa}} of the acid used) = 10(50 − 15.8), which is about 1034 using the low end of the range for methane. In energy, each {{pKa}} unit is 1.36 kcal/mol at 25 °C, so the reaction is downhill by about 34 × 1.36 = 46 kcal/mol. The notes draw equilibrium arrows because every proton transfer is in principle reversible, but with a constant this large not a single molecule of methyllithium would be left in a flask of any size. Treat it as a reaction that goes to completion.

The most common drawing mistake is to start the arrow at the metal. Arrows start at electrons. The electrons that make the new C-H bond are the pair in the C-Li (or C-Mg) bond, which the lecture treats as a lone pair on carbon. Start the arrow at that bond, or at the lone pair if you have drawn the carbanion, and end it at the hydrogen of water. The second arrow starts at the O-H bond and ends on oxygen. Lithium is a spectator: it starts as the partner of carbon and ends as the partner of hydroxide.

macro.t: Strong base means anything acidic destroys the reagent
macro.h: The comparison with water applies to every acid whose {{pKa}} is below about 50, which is nearly everything in the lecture's table: carboxylic acids (4), water (15.7), alcohols (about 16), alkynes with a C-H on the triple bond (25) and amines (38). Each of them turns R-Li or R-MgX into plain R-H. The key to Question 1D of the past exam lists this as a standard mistake: adding the acid in step 1 destroys the Grignard reagent before it can attack carbon dioxide. Acid is always a separate, later step.

why.q: Why does methyllithium react completely with water, when hydroxide and water just exchange a proton back and forth?
why.a: Hydroxide and water give the same acid on both sides, so K = 1. Methyllithium acts as the methyl anion, whose conjugate acid, methane, has a pKa of 50 to 60, far higher than water's 15.8. The equilibrium lies overwhelmingly on the side of the weaker acid, methane.

sections.title: Using the base on purpose: the synthesis homework, propene to labelled propane
sections.html:
Destroying an organometallic reagent with water sounds like a waste, but it is a clean way to put a hydrogen on one chosen carbon. The lecture sets it as a synthesis problem: the starting material is propene. Product 1 is propane with a D on the middle carbon (2-deuteriopropane). Product 2 is propane. What steps are needed?

Work backward from product 1. The D came from {{D2O}}, delivered to a carbon that was acting as {{R-}}. So the middle carbon carried a metal. The metal came from a halide, so the middle carbon carried Br. And 2-bromopropane comes from propene by adding HBr.

Step 1. Add HBr to propene. The Br goes to the middle carbon:

[[rxn:C=CC>HBr;>CC(C)Br]]

Step 2. Make the organometallic reagent, with Mg in ether (or with 2 Li):

[[rxn:CC(C)Br>Mg;diethyl ether>CC(C)[Mg]Br]]

Step 3. Add {{D2O}} for product 1, or {{H2O}} for product 2:

[[rxn:CC(C)[Mg]Br>D2O;>[2H]C(C)C]] [[rxn:CC(C)[Mg]Br>H2O;>CCC]]

The last step is the methyllithium and water mechanism again: the carbon pair takes D from D-OD exactly as it takes H from H-OH. The rule to keep: the D ends up on the carbon that carried the metal, which is the carbon that carried the halogen.

micro.t: Why HBr puts the bromine on the middle carbon
micro.h: Addition to an alkene is the first reaction type of the course. The proton of HBr adds to the double bond first and makes a carbocation. Adding H to the end carbon of propene leaves the positive charge on the middle carbon, which has two carbon groups attached and is a secondary carbocation. Adding H to the middle carbon would leave a primary carbocation on the end, which is much less stable. The reaction takes the more stable path, and bromide then attaches to the middle carbon. The result is 2-bromopropane, and it fixes where the metal, and later the D, will be.

micro.t: Why you cannot shorten the route
micro.h: It is tempting to treat propane directly with {{D2O}} and a base. That fails because a C-H bond of an alkane has a {{pKa}} of 50 to 60: no base in the flask can remove that proton to let a D take its place. The halide and the metal are the way to make that one carbon behave as a carbanion. For product 2 the same three steps apply with {{H2O}}. On paper product 2 only needs H added to both carbons of the double bond, but the homework asks you to see that one intermediate, the organometallic reagent, gives either product depending on what you add last.

macro.t: Deuterium labels in research and in medicine
macro.h: Replacing a chosen H with D is a standard way to follow one atom through a reaction or through metabolism, because D behaves chemically like H but can be told apart by mass spectrometry and by NMR. It also has a direct medical use. A C-D bond is slightly stronger than a C-H bond and is broken more slowly by the enzymes that metabolize drugs. Deutetrabenazine, approved in 2017 for the movement disorder of Huntington's disease, is a known drug with certain hydrogens replaced by deuterium so that it lasts longer in the body.

why.q: In the synthesis, why does the deuterium end up on the middle carbon and nowhere else?
why.a: Only the carbon bonded to magnesium (or lithium) is carbanion-like and able to take a D from D2O. That is the carbon that held the bromine, and HBr placed the bromine on the middle carbon of propene. Every other hydrogen in the molecule is an ordinary alkane C-H and is not touched.

sections.title: From base to nucleophile: the Grignard reagent and carbon dioxide on the past exam
sections.html:
The lecture pages show R:− acting as a base, taking a proton. The past exam, Question 1D, asks for the next step in the same idea: R:− acting as a nucleophile, giving its pair to an electron-poor carbon. The reaction is PhMgBr with 1) {{CO2}}, then 2) {{H+}}/{{H2O}}, and the product is benzoic acid.

[[rxn:Br[Mg]c1ccccc1>1) CO2;2) H3O+>OC(=O)c1ccccc1]]

The mechanism has two steps and four arrows:

[[mech:grignard-co2-benzoic-acid]]
  1. Nucleophilic attack. The electrons of the C-Mg bond (the reagent behaves as Ph:− with (MgBr)+) attack the carbon of O=C=O. At the same time the electrons of one C=O π bond move onto that oxygen. The intermediate is a carboxylate, benzoate, {{PhCO2-}} with (MgBr)+.
  2. Proton transfer in the acid workup. A lone pair on {{O-}} takes H from {{H3O+}}, and the H-O electrons stay on the oxygen of water. The product is benzoic acid, with water.

The points on the exam: correct nucleophile and electrophile with the first arrow (20), π electrons to O (10), the carboxylate intermediate with its charges (10), the protonation arrows (10), the product (5).

The mistakes the key lists: attacking an oxygen of {{CO2}}, starting the arrow from Mg, adding the acid in step 1, and forgetting the workup.

micro.t: Why the carbon of carbon dioxide is the target
micro.h: Use the Lewis acid and base language of Chapter 6. The carbon of {{CO2}} is double bonded to two oxygens, and both pull electron density away from it, so it is strongly δ+: an electron-poor site, a Lewis acid. The oxygens are δ− and have lone pairs, so a carbanion has no reason to attack them. The pair from the C-Mg bond goes to the carbon. Carbon cannot have five bonds, so as the new C-C bond forms, one π bond breaks and its pair moves onto oxygen. That second arrow is worth 10 points and is the one most often left out.

micro.t: Why the acid waits for step 2
micro.h: The numbers 1) and 2) on the arrow mean two separate operations, in order. If the acid were present from the start, the Grignard reagent would meet {{H3O+}}, {{pKa}} −1.5, and take a proton from it at once, giving benzene, R-H, and no carboxylic acid. After step 1 the carbanion is gone: its electrons are now a C-C bond. The carboxylate that remains is a weak base (its conjugate acid has {{pKa}} 4), and {{H3O+}} is a far stronger acid than that, so the proton transfer in step 2 lies completely toward benzoic acid.

macro.t: One reagent, one new carbon-carbon bond
macro.h: This reaction turns a halide into a carboxylic acid with one more carbon: bromobenzene, then PhMgBr, then benzoic acid. Building a larger carbon skeleton from smaller pieces is the central task of synthesis, and a carbon nucleophile such as a Grignard reagent is the most direct tool for it. Within this unit the reaction links three lectures: the polar C-Mg bond (10/29), the strong-base behaviour that forces the acid into a separate step (11/03), and the nucleophile and electrophile vocabulary that begins on the next page of the 11/03 notes with {{SN2}}.

why.q: In Question 1D, why would adding the acid together with the carbon dioxide ruin the reaction?
why.a: A Grignard reagent is a very strong base, and proton transfer to it from a strong acid is far faster and more favourable than anything else it can do. The reagent would be converted to benzene before it could attack carbon dioxide. Acid is added only after the new C-C bond exists, when the only base left is the carboxylate.

homework.q: Synthesis (HW): starting material propene → product 1, propane with D on the middle carbon (2-deuteriopropane); product 2, propane. What steps are needed?

steps.t: Compare product 1 with the starting material
steps.h: Propene has a C=C between the end carbon and the middle carbon. Product 1 has no double bond and has one D on the middle carbon. So one H has been added to the end carbon and one D to the middle carbon. The D has to be delivered to one specific carbon.

steps.t: Ask where a D on carbon can come from
steps.h:
From this lecture: R-Li and R-MgX act as R:− and take H from water. With {{D2O}} they take D. So the step before product 1 is an organometallic reagent with the metal on the middle carbon.
Reagent needed: {{(CH3)2CH-MgBr}} or {{(CH3)2CH-Li}}.

steps.t: Ask where the organometallic comes from
steps.h: From the 10/29 recipes: R-X + Mg in diethyl ether, or R-Br + 2 Li in pentane. The halide needed is 2-bromopropane, with Br on the middle carbon.
Add HBr to propene. The H adds to the end carbon, giving the more stable secondary carbocation on the middle carbon, and bromide attaches there: 2-bromopropane.

1. HBr. 2. Mg, diethyl ether (or 2 Li, pentane). 3. {{D2O}} for product 1.
[[rxn:C=CC>HBr;>CC(C)Br]]
[[rxn:CC(C)Br>Mg;diethyl ether>CC(C)[Mg]Br]]
[[rxn:CC(C)[Mg]Br>D2O;>[2H]C(C)C]]
Use the same first two steps and add {{H2O}} in place of {{D2O}}. The carbon takes H from water and the product is propane.

homework.answer: 1. Add HBr to propene to make 2-bromopropane. 2. Treat it with Mg in diethyl ether (or with 2 Li) to make the organometallic reagent. 3. Add D2O to get product 1, 2-deuteriopropane, or add H2O to get product 2, propane.

summary: In a C-Li or C-Mg bond the carbon is the negative end: think of R-Li as R− with Li+ and of R-MgX as R:− with (MgX)+.
In an alkyl halide such as H3C-Cl or H3C-Br the carbon is the positive end, and the bond is polar but not ionic.
Organolithium reagents are made from R-Br or R-Cl and 2 equivalents of lithium metal in pentane, giving R-Li and LiBr.
Grignard reagents are made from R-X and magnesium metal in diethyl ether, giving R-MgX.
RLi and RMgX both act as R:−, a very strong base: methyllithium and water give methane and LiOH because methane (pKa 50 to 60) is a far weaker acid than water (about 15.8).
An organometallic reagent and D2O put a D exactly where the metal, and before it the halogen, was: propene, HBr, then Mg, then D2O gives 2-deuteriopropane.
With carbon dioxide and then acid, a Grignard reagent acts as a nucleophile and gives a carboxylic acid, the mechanism of Question 1D on the past exam.
